title: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: spiral geodesic on a right cone (\kappa_g = 0) coils more closely as the cone narrows

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter X, “A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics”; topic “Geodetics of cone and ellipsoid”. Scope: high-spired gastropod shells (e.g. Turritella)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: spiral geodesic on a right cone (\kappa_g = 0) coils more closely as the cone narrows

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch10-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a precise geometric statement testable from existing 3D shell scans with standard methods. Broad enough Turritella and related material is publicly represented to confirm or refute the principal claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct high-spired shells, model the local shell envelope as a cone and compare the sutural and parallel striation paths with calculated surface geodesics. The claim is supported if their geodesic residuals are low and coil spacing decreases toward the apex as predicted.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Erosion or ornament can obscure sutures and striations.

Shell surfaces are only approximately conical.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Tightening coils on a cone are a specific alternative to a constant-pitch helix or to the shell's own logarithmic spiral, and both photographs and scans of Turritella-like shells are public. Coverage is good for common high-spired genera and thinner for the full diversity of turreted forms. Fitting the curve is a standard morphometric job on the order of weeks.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Unroll or fit the suture and parallel striae of high-spired shells such as Turritella on a cone and test whether they are conical geodesics whose coils tighten toward the apex. A constant-pitch helix, or coils that do not close apically, would refute the stated curve.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Photographs give a profile of the suture; a full geodesic test is more secure on 3D scans, which are fewer than photos.

Ornament and repaired breaks can locally displace the suture from the growth curve.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.7

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: fetch.py downloads the article PDF, records its SHA-256 and transcribes Tables 2-6 with pdfplumber into derived/pandita2013_turritellidae.csv (49 rows; all published ratio columns Wang:L and Wsut:L were recomputed from the transcribed measurements and agree, confirming the transcription). analysis.py computes for each of the 34 specimens with both apical angle and whorl number the maximum number of turns of a geodesic on a right cone of that apical angle, N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)), the ratio R = whorls/N_geo, the same ratio after subtracting two whorls (allowance for the protoconch/early whorls), and the apical angle that would have been needed for the observed whorl count to fit a geodesic.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least 90% of specimens have R > 1, i.e. the suture coils more times than any geodesic of the enveloping cone can, so the sutural line cannot be a conical geodesic. Between 10% and 90% is 'mixed'. If the tables cannot be retrieved or parsed, inconclusive with reason data-unavailable. The claim's first part (coils tighten toward the apex) is shared by a geodesic and by the logarithmic helico-spiral and is not discriminating; the verdict rests on the identification of the suture with a geodesic.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: median ratio of observed whorl number to the maximum number of turns a conical geodesic can make (R = N_obs / N_geo); R > 1 is impossible for a geodesic

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: R ranges from 1.63 to 3.39 across all 34 specimens (4 species); every specimen exceeds the bound

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'spiral geodetic' on a right cone is taken literally (a curve of zero geodesic curvature on the enveloping cone), and 'the sutural line ... such as Turritella ... is a geodetic of this kind' as the claim that the suture follows such a curve. The enveloping surface of a turritellid is close to a right circular cone whose apical angle is the measured alpha. The test uses only two gross measurements per shell, apical angle and whorl number, because the geodesic bound on the number of turns depends on nothing else. Whorl counts in the source include the early (protoconch/juvenile) whorls, where the cone approximation is roughest; the result is checked for sensitivity by also subtracting two whorls from every count.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Pandita, Zaim, Aswan & Rizal (2013) Relationship of Biometrical Aspect of Turritellidae with Geochronological Aspect in West Java, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6 (biometric measurements of 49 turritellid specimens from five Neogene localities)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The test refutes the identification of the suture with a geodesic of the enveloping right cone; it does not test Thompson's purely geometric statement that a conical geodesic coils more closely toward the apex (true) nor whether the suture is locally geodesic-like over a fraction of a whorl.

The bound assumes the shell envelope is a right circular cone, which is what Thompson states; real turritellid envelopes are slightly convex or concave, but the Clairaut relation on any such surface of revolution still forbids a geodesic from winding many times toward a narrowing apex unless the sides are almost parallel.

Specimens are Neogene fossils from West Java, not the type species Turritella terebra; fossil apices are often incomplete, so whorl counts are if anything underestimates, which makes the test conservative. Apical angles are the authors' gross measurements to 0.5 degree.

Whorl counts include early whorls where the cone approximation is roughest; subtracting two whorls from every count leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.

The published tables list 50 specimens in the text but 49 rows were present (Table 6 lacks a specimen 5B); 15 rows lack an apical angle and were excluded.

Transcription from the PDF needs pdfplumber (not in the standard tool list); the transcribed table is committed so analysis.py runs with pandas and numpy only.
